title: Architect Insurance and Liability: What Westchester Homeowners Should Know
excerpt: When you hire an architect for your Westchester home project, understanding insurance and liability protects your investment. Here's what homeowners need to know before signing a contract.
content:
If you're planning a home renovation in Westchester NY, you probably have questions about who's responsible if something goes wrong. Who pays if there's a construction defect? What if someone gets injured on the job? These aren't fun things to think about, but they matter.

The difference between hiring an architect versus hiring just a general contractor can affect your protection. When you work with a licensed architect in Westchester NY who also holds a general contractor license, you get a clearer chain of responsibility. That matters whether you're in Scarsdale, Pelham, or Ossining.

What Insurance Do Architects Actually Carry?

A licensed architect carries professional liability insurance, sometimes called errors and omissions coverage. This protects you if there's a design flaw that causes damage or cost overruns. Your architect should carry this whether they're designing a kitchen remodel in Bronxville or a second-story addition in Mamaroneck.

General contractors carry a different type of insurance: general liability and workers' compensation. This covers injuries on site and damage to your property during construction. When one person holds both licenses, like Silvio M. Luca at House Architecture & Construction, PLLC, you have both layers of protection working together.

You should always ask to see proof of insurance before work begins. It's a reasonable request. Any professional will have no problem showing you their current certificates.

Why the Design-Build Model Matters for Liability

The design-build approach in Westchester means your architect is also your contractor. That eliminates a common problem: finger-pointing between two separate companies when something goes wrong. If the architect designed it and the contractor is building it, and they're the same person, accountability is crystal clear.

This is especially important on complex projects like historic restorations in Tarrytown or Hastings-on-Hudson, where design decisions directly impact construction quality. Your architect runs the project personally, so there's no miscommunication between design and execution.

A residential architect in Scarsdale or anywhere else in Westchester County should be able to explain exactly how they protect your interests. Ask about their process for managing site inspections, quality control, and how they handle changes or disputes.

Permits and Liability in Your Municipality

Every town in Westchester, from White Plains to Rye to Eastchester, has its own building department and permit process. Your architect and contractor need to know these local codes and requirements. Pulling permits properly protects you legally.

When your architect holds both licenses, they understand the permit landscape across all Westchester municipalities. They know what Harrison's building inspector wants to see versus what New Rochelle requires. This local expertise reduces delays and prevents costly corrections later.

Make sure your contract specifies who handles permit applications, who pays permit fees, and who's responsible if work doesn't pass inspection. These details matter for home additions in Westchester and any other project type.
